summary: Embramine is a first-generation (ethanolamine-class) H1-antihistamine, structurally a brominated analogue of diphenhydramine. It is NOT FDA-approved; it is an older/regional antihistamine, so dosing and indications follow non-US product information rather than US labeling. Like other ethanolamine antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate) it competitively blocks the histamine H1 receptor to relieve allergic symptoms such as itching, urticaria and rhinitis, and it can be used for motion sickness; it has marked sedative and anticholinergic effects. Because it crosses into the central nervous system, expected effects include drowsiness, dizziness and impaired alertness, and anticholinergic effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation and urinary retention. It should be used cautiously (or avoided) in the elderly, in narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy/urinary retention, and with alcohol or other CNS depressants.

moa: Embramine is an ethanolamine-class first-generation H1-antihistamine. It competitively and reversibly antagonizes histamine at peripheral and central H1 receptors, preventing histamine-mediated increases in vascular permeability, smooth muscle contraction, pruritus and vasodilation that underlie allergic symptoms. Being lipophilic and crossing the blood-brain barrier, it produces sedation; it also has anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity, which contributes both to its anti-motion-sickness/antiemetic effect (depressing vestibular and chemoreceptor trigger zone input) and to side effects such as dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention.

preg: There are limited data on embramine in pregnancy. As a first-generation antihistamine, use only if clearly needed and at the lowest effective dose, weighing benefits against potential risks; follow regional product guidance.
lact: Antihistamines can be excreted into breast milk and may cause sedation, irritability or feeding problems in the infant; first-generation agents may also reduce milk supply. Use with caution or avoid during breastfeeding.
renal: No specific renal dosing data are available; use the lowest effective dose and monitor for accumulation of anticholinergic/sedative effects in renal impairment.
hepatic: Embramine is metabolized in the liver; use with caution in hepatic impairment, where clearance may be reduced and sedative effects prolonged.

missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule; do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose produces an anticholinergic toxidrome with central nervous system effects ranging from sedation to agitation, hallucinations, fever, flushing, dry mucous membranes, dilated pupils, urinary retention, tachycardia, and in severe cases seizures and cardiac arrhythmias (children are particularly susceptible to excitation). There is no specific routine antidote; treatment is supportive with airway/cardiac monitoring, control of seizures with benzodiazepines, and management of hyperthermia and arrhythmias; activated charcoal may be considered for recent large ingestions.
